responses.answer:

“Well, I think a lot of these views come from people’s own experiences, and some from what they hear second‑hand. Some of it makes sense to me, and some of it needs more straight facts instead of fear or guesswork.

I do think it’s true that immigrants fill jobs that are hard to staff. I’ve seen that with my own eyes. Farm work, caregiving, food service—those jobs don’t magically get done. So I understand folks who say immigrants keep parts of the economy going.

And the cultural diversity part? Honestly, I think that can be a good thing. New foods, new traditions, new ideas—it keeps the country from getting stale. You don’t have to love every change, but variety isn’t a threat by itself.

Where I think people get nervous is when life feels unstable. If someone’s struggling to pay bills or worried about their kids’ future, they look for reasons. And it’s easy to say, ‘Well, maybe it’s because too many newcomers are arriving.’ I get why that fear pops up, but that’s one of the areas where I’d want more real facts, not rumors. I don’t buy into the idea that immigrants automatically raise crime or cause terrorism risks. Those kinds of stories get tossed around a lot, but most of the time, when you dig into them, they’re not what they seemed. People deserve safety, yes, but you have to be careful not to blame whole groups without solid evidence.

On the humanitarian side—refugees, people fleeing terrible situations—that always tugged at her heart. She believed you don’t turn your back on people escaping danger. But she also believed the system has to be organized, not chaotic, so communities can absorb newcomers without falling apart.

As for jobs and income, she’d say this: ‘I get the fear, because wages have been flat and costs keep rising. But I want someone to show me clearly when immigration is the cause and when it’s companies or policies squeezing workers.’ She always felt that working people—local or immigrant—were more often in the same boat than not.

So in short, the viewpoints she found reasonable were:
– immigrants filling needed jobs  
– cultural contributions  
– concern about fair job competition, if it’s based on real economic pressures  
– wanting an orderly, well‑managed system  
– helping genuine refugees  

And the viewpoints she thought needed more facts or careful discussion were:
– claims about immigrants causing higher crime  
– sweeping statements about terrorism  
– blaming immigration alone for wage issues  

She wasn’t dismissive of anyone’s feelings, but she believed feelings shouldn’t be the whole story. She’d say, ‘Let’s talk it through, let’s look at what’s real, and let’s not jump to conclusions about people we barely know.’ That was very her.”

– bring in workers where there’s real demand,  
– set manageable limits so communities can keep up,  
– protect wages and working conditions for everyone,  
– and keep the system humane and predictable.

That, to me, feels like fairness—steady, practical, respectful to both the people already here and the people who want to build a life here.”

But at the end of the day, it’s hard to see neighbors, friends, or even your own kids lose out on work that used to be available, especially in industries like construction, factories, or service jobs that a lot of working-class people rely on.

So for me, fairness looks like making sure local folks get first shot at the available jobs, especially if they’re qualified and willing to do the work. Maybe that means employers should have to prove they couldn’t find a local worker before hiring from outside. At the same time, I don’t think we should be cruel or shut the door completely—there are jobs that are really hard to fill, and sometimes migrant workers are the only ones willing or able to do them. In those cases, I get it.

But the balance has to tilt towards the people who are already part of the community, especially when things are tight. That’s what I think is fair. And I think it’s reasonable to expect that, if someone does come from outside, they try to fit in, follow the rules, and contribute just like anybody else. That doesn’t mean giving up who they are, but it does mean respecting the community they’re joining.

That’s just the way it is. In some places, if it weren’t for immigrant workers, those businesses might close. So I get why people say they’re vital for the economy. That’s reasonable to me.

I also understand the argument about diversity adding something good to society—new foods, new celebrations, different perspectives. I’ve seen that in my own town; some of the best restaurants now are run by people who moved here from other countries. It makes life richer. So I don’t dismiss those benefits.

Now, on the other hand, security worries aren’t just made up—when you don’t know who’s coming in, or if the system isn’t careful, there can be real risks. Most people aren’t out to cause trouble, but you hear stories about crime or even terrorism, and that sticks with folks. I think those concerns are valid, but they need to be backed up by facts, not just fear or rumors. Sometimes the media makes things sound worse than they are, so I’d want to see real numbers about crime rates, not just one-off stories.

When it comes to social tensions, I think that’s real too. If large numbers of newcomers arrive quickly, it can make local people feel uneasy or even resentful, especially if they think jobs or resources are being stretched thin. I don’t think those feelings should be ignored or called prejudice right away—it’s natural to worry when things change fast. Dialogue helps, but respect on both sides is needed.

Humanitarian reasons—helping refugees or people in real need—I do believe in that, to a point. If someone’s escaping danger or poverty, I wouldn’t want to turn my back, but I think there has to be limits. We can’t fix every problem in the world, and we have to make sure we’re not hurting the people already here.

The biggest thing for me is, a lot of these arguments sound reasonable, but they need real evidence. Are immigrants really taking jobs away, or are they filling gaps? Is crime really up because of newcomers, or is that just talk? I think decisions should be made based on facts, not just feelings.

So, I find most of those viewpoints understandable, but I’d want to see more concrete proof before making big decisions. And no matter what, people on all sides should be able to talk it out, not just yell at each other. That’s the only way to find solutions everyone can live with.

As Character05_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m being honest, I wouldn’t go for complete openness—that just doesn’t seem realistic or fair, especially to people who are already struggling here. At the same time, slamming the door shut and refusing entry to everyone from outside doesn’t feel right either. I know there are situations where we need workers, or where someone truly needs a safe place.

So, I’d probably support something in the middle—admitting people based on job demand, but also setting some reasonable numerical limits. For example, if there’s a real shortage in certain industries, I think it makes sense to bring in workers to fill those gaps. But I’d want proof that those jobs really can’t be filled by people already here. Employers shouldn’t just bring in cheaper labor to save on wages or avoid hiring locals.

I also think we should keep room for genuine refugees and people in serious need, but within a system that’s controlled and managed. Maybe a cap on the number, so we’re not overwhelmed and people are given a fair chance to settle in and succeed.

For me, fairness means making sure decisions are based on what the country actually needs, not just what’s easy for businesses or what politicians say will get them votes. And social integration is just as important as the numbers—if people come here, they should get support to learn the language, understand the laws, and be part of the community, not just left to fend for themselves or live in separate worlds. That’s how you avoid resentment and help everyone get along.

So in short: focus on job demand with checks, have numerical limits overall, and keep a place for real humanitarian cases—but manage it all so the system stays fair to both newcomers and the folks already here. That’s the kind of policy I’d stand behind.

I think I’d need to see more examples of how cultural diversity has worked well in practice to feel completely comfortable with it.

Now, concerns about security—crime, social tensions, and terrorism—would definitely make me pause. I wouldn’t want to jump to conclusions or stereotype anyone, but I’d feel like it’s a valid worry to make sure immigration policies don’t inadvertently put people at risk. I’d think, "We need strong vetting processes to make sure the people coming in are here for the right reasons." But I’d also want to see the facts. If someone claimed that immigration was leading to more crime or terrorism, I’d want to know: what do the numbers actually say? Are we talking about isolated incidents, or is there a larger trend? I’d feel it’s important not to let fear take over, but I’d also believe it’s the government’s job to prioritize safety while being fair.

The humanitarian side of immigration—offering opportunities to refugees or people from impoverished regions—is something I’d feel torn about. On one hand, I’d believe in helping people in need—especially those fleeing war or persecution. I’d think, "If I were in their shoes, I’d hope someone would give me a chance." I’ve seen how hard it is for people to find good-paying jobs, and I’d feel like it’s a real concern if immigration is putting downward pressure on wages or making it harder for locals to find work. I’d say, "Let’s look at the data and make sure we’re addressing the real issues, not just pointing fingers."

So, to sum it up, I’d find a lot of these perspectives reasonable in their own way, but I’d also feel like some of them need more evidence or dialogue. I’d want to see clear data on things like crime rates, job impacts, and resource availability. And I’d want to have honest conversations about finding a balance—between helping those in need, keeping communities safe and stable, and ensuring fairness for everyone, both local and immigrant. For me, it’s not about choosing one side or the other; it’s about finding a way to make it work for the whole country.

So, the balance for me would be managing numbers, focusing on jobs where there’s real demand, and making sure that both locals and immigrants are treated fairly—whether it’s through wages, access to resources, or opportunities to succeed. responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character05_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
*settling into the conversation, speaking as Character05_F would*

You know, fairness to me has always been about everyone playing by the same rules. I grew up in a time when if you worked hard, showed up every day, and did right by your neighbors, you could count on having a decent life. That's what fairness looks like - when effort gets rewarded and people who've been here, who've put in their time and paid their dues, they get first consideration.

Community... *pauses thoughtfully* ...community is knowing the people on your street, shopping at the same stores for years, having roots somewhere. It's when your kids go to school with kids whose grandparents grew up here too. There's a comfort in that shared understanding, you know? Everyone knows what's expected, what the traditions are.

And belonging - well, that comes from being part of something bigger than yourself, but something you helped build. I remember when our neighborhood had block parties every summer, when we all knew each other's business in a good way. People looked out for each other because we were all in it together.

What worries me now is that sense of belonging getting diluted. When things change too fast, when there's too many people who don't share that same investment in the community... it makes you feel like a stranger in your own home sometimes. That's not fair to folks like us who've been the backbone of these places for generations.

*looking around the garden thoughtfully*

But sitting here, watching everyone... *sighs* ...it's not the same as it used to be. Used to be, you'd nod to Mrs. Henderson over there by the tomatoes, chat about the weather with Bob from down the street. Now there's languages I don't recognize, customs I don't understand. 

Don't get me wrong - some of these folks are perfectly nice. That young mother with the little ones, she always smiles and waves. But when I try to make conversation and we can barely understand each other... it makes you feel like an outsider in your own neighborhood.

And then there's the ones who... well, let's just say they don't seem to care much about keeping up the standards we've always had here. The loud music late at night, not maintaining their yards the way we always have. It feels disrespectful, like they don't value what we've built here.

I'm not saying I'm better than anyone, but there's a way things have always been done in this community. When that gets lost... when you feel like you have to watch what you say or walk on eggshells around your own neighbors... that's not the America I grew up in.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character05_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*leaning forward, voice getting more animated*

I've watched good, hardworking people in this community - people who were born here, whose families have been here for generations - lose their jobs or see their wages pushed down because employers would rather hire someone who'll work for half the pay and no benefits. That's not right.

My neighbor's son, he's been looking for work in construction for months. Meanwhile, there's crews of guys who don't even speak English getting hired because they'll work for peanuts. How is that fair to a young man who grew up here, went to school here, whose grandfather fought in Vietnam for this country?

And it's not just the jobs themselves - it's what it does to wages for everyone. When you've got people willing to work for next to nothing, living ten to a house, sending most of their money somewhere else... that drives down what employers think they need to pay. The rest of us can't compete with that and still pay rent and put food on the table.

Look, I understand people want better lives. But we've got our own people struggling - veterans who can't get work, single mothers trying to make ends meet, older folks like me who got pushed out of jobs before we were ready to retire. 

Fairness means we take care of them first. Once every American who wants to work has a decent job at decent wages, then maybe we can talk about bringing in more workers. But not before.

Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*settling back, speaking with the weight of experience*

Well, I've heard all these arguments, and some make more sense than others to me.

The labor shortage thing - I'm skeptical. Every time I hear "jobs Americans won't do," I think back to when I was younger. Americans did all those jobs just fine when employers had to pay decent wages. My first job was cleaning hotel rooms, and plenty of us did that work when it paid enough to live on. Now they say Americans won't do it, but maybe Americans just won't do it for slave wages.

As for cultural diversity bringing "vitality" - honestly, that sounds like something rich folks in their gated communities say. They're not the ones watching their neighborhoods change completely, where you don't recognize the place you grew up anymore. There's something to be said for stability, for traditions that have worked for generations.

Now, the security concerns... *nods grimly* ...those are real. You see what's happening in some cities, and you have to ask questions. We don't know who's coming in, especially with the border situation. And yes, I know most people are just looking for work, but it only takes a few bad apples to cause real problems.

The humanitarian angle - look, I'm not heartless. If someone's truly fleeing for their life, that's different. But there's got to be limits. We can't save the whole world, and we shouldn't destroy our own communities trying to.

What bothers me most is how anyone who raises these concerns gets called names. We should be able to have an honest conversation about what's best for Americans - all Americans - without being told we're terrible people for wanting to put our own country first.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character05_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*taking a deep breath, speaking with conviction*

Complete openness? That's just crazy talk. No country can survive with its borders wide open - that's not even a real option.

And refusing everyone? Well, that might sound appealing some days when I'm frustrated, but I know we've always had some immigration, and some of it has worked out fine when it was done right.

If I had to choose, I'd want tight numerical limits - much tighter than what we have now - combined with really strict requirements about who gets in. And I mean *really* strict.

First off, we should only let in people when there's a genuine need that can't be filled by Americans. Not "Americans won't do this job," but Americans literally can't do it - like if we need more doctors or engineers and we truly don't have enough. And even then, they should have to prove they speak English well and understand our way of life.

The numbers should be low enough that people have time to actually assimilate - not just learn the language, but really become American. When you have too many coming too fast, they just stick with their own groups and never really join the community.

And here's the thing - anyone who comes here should have to wait in line like everyone else, follow all the rules, and prove they can support themselves without taking benefits away from Americans who need them.

Most importantly, we need to actually enforce whatever rules we set. What's the point of having immigration laws if we're not going to follow them? That just makes honest people feel like suckers for playing by the rules.

The goal should be making sure America stays America, you know?

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character05_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… if I’m being Character05_F here, then let me just say it like she would’ve—plain and from the heart.

Fairness? That was something she brought up all the time, especially later in life. Not fairness like in textbooks or politics, but real fairness—the kind you feel when you’re standing in line at the grocery store, or waiting on a disability check, or watching someone move ahead not because they worked harder, but ‘cause they knew somebody, or came from somewhere else, or played the system better. She believed people should get what they earned. Not handouts. Not punishment either—but a fair shake. She didn’t mind helping folks, not at all. But she’d say, “Help shouldn’t mean forgetting about the people already here, the ones who’ve been grinding for years.”

Belonging… that one cut deep for her. She grew up in a town that used to feel like *hers*. Same faces, same church picnics, same diner where the waitress knew your order. Over the years, that changed. Not always bad, but… different. And she’d admit—she didn’t always feel like she belonged in her own neighborhood anymore. Not because she hated difference, but because it felt like no one was asking how people like her were feeling. Like their worries didn’t matter. Like loving your community and wanting it to stay *familiar* was suddenly the same as being hateful. That hurt. She wasn’t racist—not in her bones—but she wanted to be able to say, “I miss how things were,” without being called a bigot.

Community, to her, meant knowing your neighbor. Really knowing them. Not just smiling and nodding, but checking on them when it snows, bringing soup when someone’s sick, pitching in after a storm. She volunteered at the food pantry for fifteen years. Knew half the people by name. That’s where she saw things—the single mom working two jobs, the veteran sleeping in his car, the new family from Somalia who showed up confused, scared, but proud. She helped them too. But she’d sigh and say, “We can’t keep adding people without asking if we’ve got room to truly take care of ’em—all of us.”

One memory that stood out? There was a town meeting once, about housing refugees. The council said it was our moral duty. And she raised her hand—quietly, respectfully—and asked, “What about the American kids in overcrowded schools? What about the homeless vets under the highway?” No one answered her. They just said she lacked compassion. That stuck with her. Made her feel invisible. Like her version of community didn’t count anymore.

So yeah… fairness, belonging, community—they weren’t abstract ideas. They were tied up in the daily grind, in pride, in loss, in love for a way of life that felt like it was slipping away. She wanted everyone to have a place. But she also wanted to make sure the people who’d been holding the line all along didn’t get erased in the process.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character05_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*sighs softly, hands resting on knees as if sitting on a worn wooden bench in the sun*

I come to this garden most mornings with my coffee. Used to be it was just Mrs. Langley from two streets over, tending her roses, and Frank, the retired mechanic, fussing over his tomatoes. Now… well, it’s different.

There’s a young Somali woman—Amina—she’s got three kids, always so polite, keeps her plot neat as a pin. Grows these herbs I’ve never seen before. Smell like sunshine and spice. She offered me some once—said they help with digestion. I didn’t know what to say, so I took them. Made tea. Tasted funny, but I drank it anyway. We don’t talk much, but we nod. Smile. And that counts for something.

Then there’s Javier and Luis, the couple from Puerto Rico who live in the little blue house. They fixed up their yard themselves—built trellises, painted the fence. Play salsa music sometimes while they work. Loud, sure, but… you can’t help but tap your foot. They brought me a plate of mofongo last winter when I had pneumonia. That meant something.

But then… there’s others. Like Dave—the guy down by the creek path, always drinking out of a paper bag. Sometimes he’s okay, mutters hello. Other times, he yells at nothing, throws bottles. Scared the grandkids last time I brought them by. And across the way, that group living in the converted garage—three men, came here from who-knows-where, working temp jobs, I guess. Never see ’em during the day. Lights on late. Police were there once, over a fight. No arrests, but… it made me nervous.

And I won’t lie—I see folks speaking languages I don’t understand, praying in ways I don’t recognize, raising kids without what *I* call structure… and part of me pulls back. Not because I think they’re bad people. But because it feels like we don’t share the same rules anymore. Like we’re all living side by side, but not *together*.

I want to be kind. I try to be. But “diversity,” as they call it on TV—it ain’t just warm feelings and festivals. It’s real life. It’s wondering if your granddaughter can walk home safe. It’s seeing the clinic overwhelmed, the school handing out translation sheets for twelve languages, and thinking: *Who’s helping us keep up?*

I don’t fear people because they’re different. I fear what happens when no one teaches newcomers how to fit in—or worse, when we stop expecting them to. And I fear that folks like me—the ones born here, struggling, trying to do right—are supposed to just swallow our worries and smile.

But still… I stay in the garden. I wave. I bring extra seedlings to Amina in spring. Because community isn’t about agreeing on everything. It’s about showing up—even when it’s awkward. Even when you miss the old ways.

That’s what she’d say, anyway. Character05_F. She believed in showing up.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
You know… sitting here with my hands in the dirt, I’ve learned a few things. One is this: nobody’s life is simple. Not mine, not yours, and sure as heck not the folks down the block.

I’ll be honest—I grew up thinking there was a right way to live. Church on Sunday. Married before babies. Work hard, keep your word, don’t lean on the system. And for years, that’s how I judged people—quietly, maybe, but I did. Then life happened. My nephew got hooked on pills after a back injury. My best friend from high school came out at 58—nearly lost her family over it. And I had to ask myself: *Who am I to decide whose struggle counts?*

So when I see a couple living together, unmarried, raising kids—it stings a little, old habits die hard—but I think of my sister, who waited till she was 40 to have a baby, all alone, working nights, and no one called *her* immoral. Love’s love. Kids need stability, not sermons.

Same with alcoholism. Dave—the man by the creek—he wasn’t always like that. I found out he lost two sons in a car wreck. Two. And the grief just… drowned him. Do I want him yelling at night or leaving trash everywhere? No. But do I wish someone had reached out sooner, instead of letting him rot on the edges? Yes. That’s not tolerance—that’s basic human decency.

And the ones with diseases—HIV, hepatitis, whatever—look, I was scared at first. Didn’t understand. Thought you could catch it from sharing a bench. Ignorant, I know. But then I volunteered at the clinic and met people—hardworking people—who’d been cast off because of stigma. One woman, Latina, told me she didn’t go to the doctor for two years ‘cause she thought they’d treat her like trash. Broke my heart. We’ve gotta do better. Compassion isn’t weakness. It’s strength.

But—and this is where I get stuck—compassion has to go both ways.

I see newcomers sometimes, and they keep to themselves. Don’t join meetings. Don’t learn English. Send their kids to school who can’t speak a word of English, and expect the teachers to carry the load. Or they build places of worship in residential zones, park everywhere, throw loud events at midnight. And when folks complain, they say we’re “intolerant.” That cuts deep.

Tolerance? Sure. I’ll tolerate a lot—for peace. But respect? That’s earned. And integration? That’s a two-way street.

I remember one time, a group wanted to turn the community center into a shelter for migrant workers. Temporary, they said. I asked: Who cleans up? Who handles noise, or crime, or medical issues? They looked at me like I was against helping. But I wasn’t! I just wanted to know if *we*—the people already here, the ones paying taxes, trying to keep this place safe—were part of the conversation. Not afterthoughts.

So yes, more communication’s needed. Not just posters in three languages. Real talks. Over coffee, in churches, at schools. Where people like me can say, “I’m afraid,” without being called a bigot. And where new neighbors can say, “We’re scared too,” without being seen as takers.

And tolerance? Yeah, we all need more of it. But not one-sided. I’ll meet you halfway—but don’t erase me while you’re preaching unity.

Because everyone deserves to feel comfortable in their own neighborhood. Even the old white lady who still says “bless you” when you sneeze.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character05_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*sits up a little straighter, voice low but firm, like she’s been over this in her head too many times*

Fairness? When jobs are scarce… fairness means *first come, first served*—not in a mean way, but in a *who’s been holding it down* kind of way.

I worked at the same factory for twenty-three years. Started on the line, never missed a shift, even when my back gave out and I had to stand with a brace. Made less than a decent wage, but I showed up. Paid my taxes. Didn’t ask for handouts. And then they shut it down. Moved the work overseas. Then a few years later, they open a new warehouse on the edge of town—hiring fast, hiring lots—and half the people walking in are migrants, some here legally, some I’m not so sure about. And they’re taking jobs at lower pay, saying they’re “grateful for the opportunity.” 

Well, what about *us*? The ones who stayed through the hard winters, watched our schools close, our hospitals cut staff? We didn’t leave. We stuck around. And now we’re supposed to compete with people who’ll work longer hours for less, just ‘cause they’re desperate?

That ain’t fair.

Now, don’t get me wrong—I’m not against immigrants working. Hard work isn’t owned by any one group. But when there’s only so much pie, and you keep adding people to the table without making the pie bigger… someone goes hungry. And nine times out of ten, it’s folks like me—older workers, no college degree, stuck in towns that ain’t coming back—who end up on the outside looking in.

Fairness, to me, means that if you’re going to bring in migrant workers, you do it *after* you’ve taken care of your own. The people born here, raised here, paid into the system their whole lives. They should be first in line for jobs, training programs, apprenticeships. Not last.

And if there’s still need—*real* labor shortages, not just cheap labor excuses—then fine. Bring people in. But do it right. Legal. Transparent. With rules. No undercutting wages. No letting employers play one group against another. That’s how you breed resentment. That’s how good people start hating each other for things that ain’t their fault.

I remember when they brought in H-2B workers for the meatpacking plant. Locals couldn’t get hired—plant said they “weren’t reliable.” But those same locals had kids in school, couldn’t work midnight shifts. Meanwhile, the migrants lived ten to a trailer, no heat, no privacy, scared to complain. That’s exploitation—on both sides. Of them, and of us.

So balance? Balance means: protect the community that’s already here—its workers, its wages, its stability—*before* you expand it. Train the people who’ve been left behind. Invest in *our* comeback. Then, if there’s room, welcome others in a way that doesn’t pit neighbor against neighbor.

Because when jobs are tight, and money’s tight, and hope’s tight… people notice who’s getting help. And if it’s always someone else, while you’re told to stay quiet and be “inclusive,” well… that eats at the soul of a place. Tears apart the very community everyone claims to want to build.

She believed in helping people. But she also believed that a country, a town, a neighborhood—it has limits. And loyalty—to those who’ve stood by it—that matters too.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character05_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*sits back, pulls a light sweater tighter around her shoulders, voice measured now—more reflective, like she’s weighing each word before it leaves her mouth*

When you zoom out… when it’s not just our garden or the town meeting, but the whole country—I get that there’s more to this than just how I feel on my block. I know that.

And I’ll say this straight: some of what people say about immigrants? It helps. No question. My sister’s nurse in the VA clinic? From the Philippines. Kind, skilled, works twelve-hour shifts. The mechanic who keeps my car running? Guatemalan. Honest. Doesn’t overcharge. And yeah, they’re filling jobs a lot of folks here don’t want—nursing homes, farms, meat plants, cleaning crews. Hard work. Dirty. Low pay. So if they’re doing it, and doing it right, then bless ‘em. That part? Reasonable. Makes sense.

And the cultural stuff—okay, I’ll admit it. When I go to the grocery store now, I see foods I never heard of. Hear music in languages I don’t understand. Kids with names I can’t pronounce. Part of me misses the familiar. But another part thinks… maybe it keeps things alive. Keeps us from getting too stale. Towns like mine were dying—empty storefronts, no kids on bikes. Then a few families move in, open a little market, start a festival, suddenly there’s life again. I saw that in Millerton last year. Didn’t fix everything, but… it helped. So yeah, diversity *can* bring vitality. If it’s real—not forced, not flashy, but rooted.

But then we get to the other side—the worries. And don’t you dare tell me they’re all made up.

Crime? Not saying every immigrant’s a criminal. Of course not. But I’ve read the reports. I’ve seen the news. There’s folks coming across the border who’ve got records—gang ties, drugs, violence—and they’re not being checked. Or released into communities with no follow-up. My cousin’s in Tucson. Says the local jail’s overwhelmed. Sheriff says half the inmates are undocumented. Is that fair to the people living there? To their safety?

And social tension? Walk through certain neighborhoods now. Schools teaching seven different curriculums to keep everyone “included.” Public signs in five languages, but nothing in English first. PTA meetings where half the parents don’t speak the language, so decisions get made by a few loud voices or outsiders. And the rest of us? We sit quiet, because if we say *anything*, we’re called racists. That’s tension. Real tension. Not hate—but confusion. Like we’re losing shared ground.

Terrorism? That one makes me nervous saying it out loud. Feels extreme. But after 9/11, after Boston, after all of it—you learn not to ignore the cracks in the system. If we don’t vet properly, if borders are wide open and nobody’s asking questions, then yes, I worry. Not that every refugee’s a threat. But that one bad apple, slipping through… and the cost is too high.

Humanitarian reasons—refugees, people fleeing war or poverty—that tugs at me. I’m not heartless. No child should starve. No woman should run from soldiers burning her village. But here’s where I get stuck: when we pour help overseas—when we welcome thousands from far away—while our own veterans sleep under bridges, our own kids go to bed hungry, our own disabled neighbors can’t afford medicine… it feels backwards. Like we care more about strangers in crisis than the people who built this country.

And the fear about jobs and wages? That’s not fear. That’s fact. I’ve lived it. When employers can hire people for less—because they’re desperate, because they’re temporary, because they won’t complain—they will. And then the rest of us have to compete with that. Wages go down. Benefits vanish. Jobs become unstable. That’s not conspiracy. That’s economics. And it hits people like me—older, without degrees, tied to one town—hardest.

So which views are reasonable?

All of ‘em—except the ones that pretend the other side doesn’t suffer.

The worker needing a job. The refugee needing safety. The community needing order. The taxpayer wondering where the limits are.

What needs more facts? The crime stats—real data, not headlines. Not “they’re all criminals” or “none of them are”—just truth. How many are actually arrested? For what? Are certain policies making it harder to track? And integration numbers—how many learn English? How many stay long-term? Pay taxes? Become self-sufficient?

And dialogue? Lord knows we need that. Not shouting matches on TV. Not politicians using us as props. But real talks—in churches, libraries, union halls—where people like me can say, “I’m scared I’m being forgotten,” and newcomers can say, “We’re scared too—we just want a chance.” Without either side being labeled.

She always said: “You can care about your own *and* care about others. Just don’t make one invisible to save the other.”

That’s what’s missing now. Balance. Memory. Respect—for everyone, not just the loudest or the newest.

responses.answer:
*leans forward, hands clasped, voice quieter now—more certain, like she’s arrived at something after years of turning it over in her mind*

Complete openness? No. As kind as I want to be, no. You can’t just open the door and say “come one, come all” when schools are overcrowded, clinics are underfunded, and half the working people in this town are one paycheck from disaster. That’s not compassion—that’s chaos. And chaos hurts everyone, including the very people we’re trying to help.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That’s too hard. Too closed. We’ve always had newcomers—my own great-grandfather came from Ireland with nothing but a suitcase and a cough. And like I said, some jobs *aren’t* being filled. So shutting the door completely? No. That ain’t who we are.

So if I’m choosing… I’d go with **job-based admission**, but *only* after we’ve made sure local workers—especially those in struggling communities like mine—have been given first shot. Retraining. Support. Real chances. Not just a pamphlet and a website nobody can navigate.

And yes—**set numerical limits**. Clear ones. Based on what our towns can actually absorb. Not what some politician says will win votes, or what big business wants to keep wages low. Limits that consider housing, schools, hospitals, infrastructure. If we don’t have room to integrate people properly—to help them learn English, find stable work, become part of the community—then we don’t have room. Period.

And here’s what I’d add: **integration must be required**, not optional.  
You want to come here to work? Fine. But you learn English. You follow the laws. You respect the culture—not by giving up your own, but by adding to ours, not replacing it. You pay taxes. You don’t live ten families to a house, creating health hazards. And you don’t get benefits—welfare, housing, free college—before citizens do. That’s fairness.

Temporary worker programs? Okay—but they stay *temporary*. No backdoor paths to permanent status unless the system verifies real need *and* full compliance. And employers? Fined heavy if they exploit them or use them to undercut American workers. No more playing one group against another.

As for refugees—humanitarian cases—yes, we should help. But in numbers we can manage. And placed where communities agree to take them, not dumped in towns already struggling without warning or support. Let people vote—yes or no—in their counties. Call it respect.

And borders? Secure them. Not cruelly. Not by locking kids in cages. But by having rules, and guards, and processing centers that work. So people aren’t sneaking through in the dark, risking lives, or bringing danger with them. A legal path, clear and open—if slow—so desperation doesn’t become the only way in.

That’s the balance she believed in: **compassion with order. Openness with limits. Kindness with responsibility.**

Not blind welcome. Not cold rejection. But a nation that helps others—*after* it protects its own, and *while* making sure new neighbors become part of the fabric, not threads pulling it apart.

She used to say, “A home is only strong if the door isn’t broken.” You can open it wide for guests—but only if the frame still holds. Otherwise, everybody ends up out in the cold.

*sits quietly for a long moment, hands resting in her lap, eyes lowered—then slowly looks up, voice softer now, more like J again*

You know… I thought I knew her well. I *did* know her—over thirty years of friendship, church potlucks, hospital visits, funerals we stood through side by side. But doing this—speaking as her, not about her—it made me feel something I hadn’t before.

I realized how much pain was underneath her words. Not bitterness, not hate—but grief. Grief for a world that changed without asking people like her if they were ready. She wasn’t afraid of immigrants because they were foreign. She was afraid of becoming foreign in her own life.

And while I’ve always leaned more open—more hopeful, maybe naïve—I see now that her concerns weren’t just “those of an older white woman who didn’t get with the times.” They were the worries of someone who worked hard, played by the rules, and felt the ground shift while she was still standing on it. She didn’t want special treatment—just to be seen. To matter in the story.

Embodying her… it didn’t change my belief that we should help people fleeing hardship. I still believe that. But now I feel it with a weight I didn’t before. Because helping others can’t mean erasing those already here. Compassion has to have room for everyone—not just the newest need, but the quiet, long-standing ones too.

I used to think people like her resisted change out of fear. Now I see it was also love—love for a community, a way of life, a sense of belonging that took decades to build. And when that’s washed away fast, without care or conversation, is it any wonder people hold tighter to what’s left?

So yes… I learned something. That listening doesn’t mean agreeing. But it means honoring the truth in someone’s experience—even when it challenges your own.

And maybe… maybe immigration policy isn’t just about borders or economics. Maybe it’s about dignity.  
The dignity of the refugee fleeing violence.  
And the dignity of the waitress in Ohio who raised two kids alone and wonders why no one fights for *her* future.

Character05_F wanted both to matter.  
And after today… so do I.
